title: Reading the film
text: {{1}} some countries every foreign film is dubbed by actors who become the unofficial voices of the stars, {{2}} elsewhere the audience simply reads. {{3}} dubbing is the norm, subtitles are often seen as an art-film ritual; {{4}} is the size of the American market that whole national dubbing industries grew up to serve it. Fans of subtitles argue {{5}} a film should be heard in its own language, with the actors' breath and timing intact, {{6}} dubbing fans reply that reading the bottom of the screen is not watching the film at all. There is also a quieter, practical argument for subtitles: they quietly teach reading speed, foreign vocabulary and attention. {{7}} side wins the argument, the nineteenth-century dream of cinema as a universal language has been quietly corrected: it is a household of languages, {{8}} makes the humble subtitle one of the cinema's quiet heroes.

gaps.hint: conjunction: dubbed, ___ elsewhere the audience reads
gaps.explanation: Contrast between the two customs: while.
'Where dubbing is the norm' — the elliptical place clause.

gaps.hint: pronoun: ___ is the size of the market that
gaps.explanation: Fronted inversion: 'Such is the size that…'.

gaps.hint: conjunction: argue ___ a film should be heard

gaps.explanation: Contrast between the two camps: while.
'Whichever side wins' — it does not matter which.

gaps.hint: relative: ___, __ makes the subtitle a hero
gaps.explanation: Sentential relative after the colon part; 'that' is impossible here.
